content: Elephant shrews, also known as jumping shrews, are small insectivorous mammals that are native to Africa. They belong to the family Macroscelididae within the order Macroscelidea. Their common English name, elephant shrew, originates from the resemblance of their elongated noses to an elephant's trunk and an earlier assumption of their relationship to true shrews (family Soricidae) in the order Insectivora. However, it is now understood that elephant shrews are not closely related to true shrews. As a result, some individuals prefer to call them sengis, a term derived from Bantu languages in Africa. These animals are distributed across southern Africa and can inhabit a wide range of environments, including the Namib Desert, rocky outcrops in South Africa, and dense forests. One species, the North African Elephant Shrew, is found in the semi-arid, mountainous regions of northwestern Africa. Elephant shrews exhibit a size range from approximately 100 mm to nearly 300 mm in length and weigh between just under 50 g to over 500 g. For example, the Short-eared Elephant Shrew has an average length of 150 mm. These mammals are quadrupedal, with mouse-like tails and relatively long legs for their body size. Their elongated noses, or trunks, vary in size among species but are flexible and used to search for food. Their lifespan is typically two to three years. Their diet primarily consists of insects and other small invertebrates, such as beetles, spiders, worms, ants, and termites, which they often collect from leaf litter. They also consume seeds and green plant shoots. Elephant shrews possess large canine teeth and high-crowned cheek teeth, similar to those of ungulates. Their dental formula is distinctive. Although they are mostly diurnal and highly active, elephant shrews are elusive and rarely seen. They are cautious, well-camouflaged, and capable of rapid movement to escape threats. Some species create and maintain a network of cleared pathways through undergrowth, which they patrol for insects. These pathways also serve as unobstructed escape routes when disturbed. Elephant shrews are not highly social animals, but many species form monogamous pairs that share and defend a home territory. They mark their territories using scent glands. Certain species, such as those in the genus Rhynchocyon, dig small conical holes in the soil, similar to bandicoots, while others use natural crevices or construct leaf nests. Females give birth to litters of one to three offspring multiple times per year, with a gestation period ranging from 45 to 60 days. The young are born relatively well-developed but remain in the nest for several days before venturing out. Historically, elephant shrews were classified alongside shrews and hedgehogs within the order Insectivora. They were also considered distant relatives of ungulates, grouped with treeshrews, or even included with hares and rabbits in the order Lagomorpha. However, recent molecular studies strongly support their placement within the superorder Afrotheria. This superorder unites elephant shrews with other African mammals, such as tenrecs, golden moles, hyraxes, sirenians, aardvarks, and elephants, as well as certain ungulates. Fossil evidence reveals several extinct species of elephant shrews, all originating from Africa. Some fossil species, such as Myohyrax, were so similar to hyraxes that they were initially misclassified, while others, like Mylomygale, resembled rodents. These unusual forms became extinct by the Pleistocene epoch. There are 16 recognized species of elephant shrews, divided into four genera. Two of these genera are monotypic, containing only one species each. The classification is as follows: Order Macroscelidea Family Macroscelididae Genus Elephantulus Short-snouted Elephant Shrew (Elephantulus brachyrhynchus) Cape Elephant Shrew (Elephantulus edwardii) Dusky-footed Elephant Shrew (Elephantulus fuscipes) Dusky Elephant Shrew (Elephantulus fuscus) Bushveld Elephant Shrew (Elephantulus intufi) Eastern Rock Elephant Shrew (Elephantulus myurus) Somali Elephant Shrew (Elephantulus revoili) North African Elephant Shrew (Elephantulus rozeti) Rufous Elephant Shrew (Elephantulus rufescens) Western Rock Elephant Shrew (Elephantulus rupestris) Genus Macroscelides Short-eared Elephant Shrew (Macroscelides proboscideus) Genus Petrodromus Four-toed Elephant Shrew (Petrodromus tetradactylus) Genus Rhynchocyon Golden-rumped Elephant Shrew (Rhynchocyon chrysopygus) Checkered Elephant Shrew (Rhynchocyon cirnei) Black and Rufous Elephant Shrew (Rhynchocyon petersi) Grey-faced Sengi (Rhynchocyon udzungwensis) This classification highlights the diversity within the family Macroscelididae and the unique adaptations of these fascinating mammals.
